etymologies.heading: Etymology 1
paragraphs: From Middle English mōt, ȝemōt, from Old English *mōt, ġemōt (“meeting”), from Proto-Germanic *mōtą, from Proto-Indo-European *meh₂d- (“to encounter, come”). Cognate with Scots mut, mote (“meeting, assembly”), Low German Mööt (“meeting”), Moot (“meeting”), archaic Dutch (ge)moet (“meeting”), Danish møde (“meeting”), Swedish möte (“meeting”), Norwegian møte (“meeting”), Icelandic mót (“meeting, tournament, meet”). Related to meet. The adjective derives from the noun.
senses: (current in UK, rare in the US) Subject to discussion (originally at a moot); arguable, debatable, unsolved or impossible to solve.
(Canada, US, chiefly law) Being an exercise of thought; academic.
A system of arbitration in many areas of Africa in which the primary goal is to settle a dispute and reintegrate adversaries into society rather than assess penalties.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 2
paragraphs: From Middle English moten (“to speak, talk, converse, discuss”), from Old English mōtian (“to speak, converse, discuss”), from Proto-Germanic *mōtijaną (“to meet, encounter”), a suffixed derivative of *mōtą (“meeting”). Related to etymology 1. See also mutter (which is a frequentative of moot).
senses: To bring up as a subject for debate.
(Scotland, Northern England) A whisper, or an insinuation, also gossip or rumors.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 4
senses: (West Country) The stump of a tree; the roots and bottom end of a felled tree.
(West Country) To take root and begin to grow.
(West Country) To turn up soil or dig up roots, especially an animal with a snout.

etymologies.heading: Etymology 5
paragraphs: Clipping of mutual with humorously altered pronunciation.
senses: (Internet slang, endearing, usually in the plural) A mutual follower on a social media platform.
